Notebook · Volume 3 · Autumn

Field notes from the estuary

Birds, mud and the long light of October

Arrival

The tide was already turning when I reached the sea wall, and the whole flat shone like a tray of pewter. Redshank worked the edge of the channel in ones and twos, bobbing as they walked, and further out a loose crowd of knot lifted, turned, and showed first their dark backs and then their pale bellies, so that the flock seemed to blink on and off against the sky.

I had come for the geese, which arrive in the second week of the month and are, depending on the wind, either a distant murmur or an overwhelming noise. This year they were late. Instead I got wigeon, a pair of curlew, and a heron standing so still in the shallows that for ten minutes I took it for a post.

Tide table

High water 07:42, 5.1 m.

Wind: light, west-south-west. Visibility good.

The wall at noon

By midday the mud had been uncovered for an hour, and the feeding became serious. Dunlin ran in tight packs along the waterline, each bird stitching its beak into the mud as if sewing, while above them a single peregrine hung in the wind and thought about lunch. The effect on the dunlin was dramatic: all at once they rose, wheeled, settled, and rose again. Nothing was caught. Nothing, I think, was meant to be.

The aside to the right is a list I keep pinned inside the cover of the notebook; it is not scientific, but it has saved me from several wet mistakes. Check the tide before leaving the house. Check it again at the car. Never trust a path that is darker than the one beside it.

There is no such thing as an empty estuary. There are only the hours when you have not yet learned where to look.

— a note on the inside cover, in someone else's handwriting

What I saw

  • Redshank, about thirty, working the channel edge.
  • Knot, perhaps four hundred, in one flock.
  • Wigeon, eleven, grazing the saltmarsh fringe.
  • Curlew, two, with that unmistakable downward bill.
  • Little egret, one, which did not stay.
  • Peregrine, one, which did not need to.

At the end of the afternoon I walked back along the top of the wall with the light behind me, and my own shadow ran a long way out onto the flat. The pocket recorder, which I had forgotten to switch on, was still in its case. Press Rec next time; the evening chorus was the best part of the day.

Set in a plain serif. Transcribed from a pencil notebook, with the spelling left alone.
